_note: Human-written reference text. NOT part of the BeatAML 2.0 release and not machine-verified. Molecular formula/weight/structure shown alongside this in the app come from PubChem and are authoritative; the fields here (developer, mechanism, other uses) are background summaries and should be confirmed against the linked PubChem entry or a drug label before being relied on. Keyed by the drug's primary name.

Venetoclax.developer: AbbVie (from Abbott's BCL-2 programme) with Genentech/Roche; originally ABT-199.
Venetoclax.mechanism: A BH3-mimetic: it plugs the groove on the BCL-2 protein that normally sequesters pro-death partners. Freed, those partners trigger apoptosis, so the leukemia cell executes the self-destruct programme it had been suppressing.
Venetoclax.otherUses: Approved for chronic lymphocytic leukemia and small lymphocytic lymphoma, and for AML in combination with azacitidine, decitabine or low-dose cytarabine in adults unfit for intensive chemotherapy.

Cabozantinib.mechanism: Blocks several receptor tyrosine kinases at once — MET, VEGFR2, AXL, RET, KIT and FLT3 — cutting both growth signalling and the tumour's blood supply.
Cabozantinib.otherUses: Approved for medullary and differentiated thyroid cancer, advanced renal cell carcinoma, and hepatocellular carcinoma after sorafenib.

Quizartinib.developer: Ambit Biosciences, later developed by Daiichi Sankyo.
Quizartinib.mechanism: A highly selective type II FLT3 inhibitor: it binds FLT3 only in its inactive shape, wedging the kinase shut. Because it needs that inactive conformation, it works well against FLT3-ITD but poorly against TKD mutations such as D835 that hold the kinase open.
Quizartinib.otherUses: Approved with chemotherapy for newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD-positive AML. Not used outside AML.

Sorafenib.mechanism: A multi-kinase inhibitor hitting RAF along the MAPK growth pathway plus VEGFR, PDGFR, KIT and FLT3. Like quizartinib it is a type II binder, so FLT3 TKD mutants resist it.
Sorafenib.otherUses: Approved for hepatocellular carcinoma, advanced renal cell carcinoma, and radioactive-iodine-refractory differentiated thyroid carcinoma.

Sunitinib.mechanism: Broad receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor — VEGFR, PDGFR, KIT, FLT3 and RET — combining an anti-growth effect with an anti-angiogenic one.
Sunitinib.otherUses: Approved for renal cell carcinoma, imatinib-resistant gastrointestinal stromal tumour, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours.

Midostaurin.developer: Novartis, originating in Ciba-Geigy research on staurosporine derivatives.
Midostaurin.mechanism: A type I FLT3 inhibitor — it binds the active conformation, so unlike quizartinib it retains activity against TKD mutants. Also inhibits KIT, PKC and several other kinases.
Midostaurin.chemClass: Indolocarbazole; a semi-synthetic derivative of the natural product staurosporine.
Midostaurin.otherUses: Approved with chemotherapy for FLT3-mutated AML, and for advanced systemic mastocytosis and mast cell leukemia.

Gilteritinib.mechanism: Type I FLT3 inhibitor that also blocks AXL. Because it binds the active conformation it covers both ITD and TKD (D835) mutations, which is why it is used when a type II inhibitor stops working.
Gilteritinib.otherUses: Approved for relapsed or refractory FLT3-mutated AML. Not used outside AML.

Crenolanib.developer: Originated at Pfizer, developed by AROG Pharmaceuticals.
Crenolanib.mechanism: Type I inhibitor of FLT3 and PDGFR that keeps working against D835 TKD mutants, unlike the type II drugs.
Crenolanib.otherUses: Investigational in AML and in PDGFRA-mutant gastrointestinal stromal tumour.

Ponatinib.mechanism: Designed around a carbon–carbon triple bond that lets it reach past the bulky T315I 'gatekeeper' mutation that defeats other BCR-ABL drugs. Also inhibits FLT3, KIT, FGFR and PDGFR.
Ponatinib.otherUses: Approved for chronic myeloid leukemia and Philadelphia-chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia, particularly T315I-mutant disease.

Dovitinib.mechanism: Multi-targeted receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor covering FGFR, VEGFR, PDGFR, FLT3 and KIT.
Dovitinib.otherUses: Investigated in renal cell carcinoma and other solid tumours; not approved.

Foretinib.mechanism: Inhibits MET and VEGFR2 primarily, with activity against RON, AXL, KIT and FLT3.
Foretinib.otherUses: Investigated in gastric, papillary renal and head-and-neck cancers; not approved.

Panobinostat.mechanism: Pan-histone deacetylase inhibitor. Histone deacetylases strip acetyl tags off the proteins DNA is wound around; blocking them loosens chromatin and switches large sets of genes back on, including ones that drive cell death.
Panobinostat.otherUses: Approved with bortezomib and dexamethasone for multiple myeloma after prior therapy.

Elesclomol.mechanism: A copper ionophore: it grabs copper ions and ferries them into mitochondria, where the metal overwhelms the cell with oxidative stress and triggers copper-dependent death. This is why it kills almost every sample in the panel — the mechanism is not specific to any mutation.
Elesclomol.otherUses: Failed a phase III trial in metastatic melanoma; now studied mainly as a copper-delivery tool and in copper-metabolism disease.

Selinexor.mechanism: Selective inhibitor of nuclear export. It blocks XPO1, the shuttle that carries proteins out of the nucleus, so tumour-suppressor proteins stay where they can act instead of being exported and neutralised.
Selinexor.otherUses: Approved for multiple myeloma and for relapsed or refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

Flavopiridol.developer: Derived from rohitukine, a natural product from the Indian plant Dysoxylum binectariferum; developed as alvocidib with the US National Cancer Institute.
Flavopiridol.mechanism: Inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases, especially CDK9. Blocking CDK9 stalls transcription, which rapidly depletes short-lived survival proteins such as MCL-1 that leukemia cells depend on.
Flavopiridol.otherUses: Investigated in AML and chronic lymphocytic leukemia; not approved.

SNS-032.mechanism: Selective inhibitor of CDK2, CDK7 and CDK9 — blocking both cell-cycle progression and transcription.
SNS-032.otherUses: Investigated in chronic lymphocytic leukemia and multiple myeloma; not approved.

Trametinib.developer: Discovered by Japan Tobacco, developed by GlaxoSmithKline, now Novartis.
Trametinib.mechanism: Allosteric MEK1/MEK2 inhibitor — it binds beside the ATP pocket rather than in it, locking MEK and cutting the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK growth signal one step below RAF.
Trametinib.otherUses: Approved with dabrafenib for BRAF V600-mutant melanoma, non-small-cell lung cancer, and anaplastic thyroid cancer.

Ibrutinib.developer: Celera Genomics, developed by Pharmacyclics with Janssen.
Ibrutinib.mechanism: Forms a permanent covalent bond to a cysteine in Bruton's tyrosine kinase, switching off B-cell receptor signalling for the life of the protein.
Ibrutinib.otherUses: Approved for chronic lymphocytic leukemia, mantle cell lymphoma, Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, marginal zone lymphoma and chronic graft-versus-host disease.

Entospletinib.mechanism: Selective inhibitor of spleen tyrosine kinase (SYK), a signalling hub downstream of immune receptors that some AML cells rely on.
Entospletinib.otherUses: Investigated in AML and B-cell malignancies; not approved.

JQ1.developer: James Bradner's laboratory at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, published in 2010 and released as an open chemical probe.
JQ1.mechanism: BET bromodomain inhibitor. It mimics an acetylated lysine, so BRD4 binds it instead of chromatin and falls off DNA — which shuts down transcription of MYC and other cancer-driving genes.
JQ1.otherUses: A laboratory tool compound, never developed as a medicine; it seeded the clinical BET-inhibitor field.
JQ1.activeIngredient: (+)-JQ1 — a laboratory probe, never formulated as a medicine

Bortezomib.mechanism: Reversibly blocks the 26S proteasome, the cell's protein shredder. Waste protein piles up and triggers a terminal stress response — a burden felt hardest by cells that secrete protein heavily, such as myeloma cells.
Bortezomib.otherUses: Approved for multiple myeloma and for mantle cell lymphoma.

Azacytidine.developer: First synthesised in the 1960s by Alois Pískala and František Šorm at the Czechoslovak Academy of Sciences.
Azacytidine.mechanism: A cytidine analogue that gets built into DNA, where it traps and destroys DNA methyltransferase. Methyl marks are lost as cells divide, and silenced genes switch back on.
Azacytidine.otherUses: Approved for myelodysplastic syndromes, chronic myelomonocytic leukemia and AML; a standard partner for venetoclax in older AML patients.

Lenalidomide.developer: Celgene (now Bristol Myers Squibb), as an analogue of thalidomide.
Lenalidomide.mechanism: Molecular glue: it binds cereblon, part of a protein-disposal machine, and redirects it to destroy the transcription factors IKZF1 and IKZF3 — proteins the machine would otherwise ignore.
Lenalidomide.otherUses: Approved for multiple myeloma, del(5q) myelodysplastic syndrome, mantle cell lymphoma and follicular lymphoma.

Ruxolitinib.developer: Incyte, partnered with Novartis outside the US.
Ruxolitinib.mechanism: Inhibits JAK1 and JAK2, the kinases that relay cytokine signals to STAT transcription factors — the pathway left constitutively on by JAK2 V617F.
Ruxolitinib.otherUses: Approved for myelofibrosis, polycythemia vera and steroid-refractory graft-versus-host disease.

Dasatinib.mechanism: A type I inhibitor of BCR-ABL that also hits the SRC-family kinases, KIT and PDGFR. Binding the active conformation lets it overcome many imatinib-resistant mutations.
Dasatinib.otherUses: Approved for chronic myeloid leukemia and Philadelphia-chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

Imatinib.developer: Ciba-Geigy/Novartis — Alex Matter and Nicholas Lydon's chemistry with Brian Druker's clinical work.
Imatinib.mechanism: Wedges into the inactive conformation of the BCR-ABL fusion kinase and holds it shut. Also inhibits KIT and PDGFR. It was the first targeted cancer drug to turn a fatal leukemia into a manageable condition.
Imatinib.otherUses: Approved for chronic myeloid leukemia, Ph+ acute lymphoblastic leukemia, gastrointestinal stromal tumour, hypereosinophilic syndrome and dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans.

Nilotinib.developer: Novartis, rationally redesigned from the imatinib scaffold for a tighter fit.
Nilotinib.mechanism: Type II BCR-ABL inhibitor, roughly 20-fold more potent than imatinib and active against many imatinib-resistant mutations.

Bosutinib.mechanism: Dual SRC and ABL inhibitor; notable for sparing KIT and PDGFR, which changes its side-effect profile.

Erlotinib.developer: OSI Pharmaceuticals, with Genentech and Roche.
Erlotinib.mechanism: Reversibly blocks the ATP site of the EGFR kinase, cutting the growth signal in tumours driven by EGFR mutations.
Erlotinib.otherUses: Approved for EGFR-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer and, with gemcitabine, for pancreatic cancer.

Afatinib.mechanism: Binds the ErbB family — EGFR, HER2 and HER4 — irreversibly through a covalent bond, giving longer-lasting blockade than reversible EGFR drugs.
Afatinib.otherUses: Approved for EGFR-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer.

Crizotinib.mechanism: Originally designed as a MET inhibitor; it also blocks ALK and ROS1, which became its clinical purpose after ALK fusions were found in lung cancer.
Crizotinib.otherUses: Approved for ALK-positive and ROS1-positive non-small-cell lung cancer and for ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphoma.

Palbociclib.mechanism: Inhibits CDK4 and CDK6, the kinases that release the brake protein RB and let a cell commit to division. Blocking them arrests the cell before DNA replication.
Palbociclib.otherUses: Approved with endocrine therapy for hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer.

Selumetinib.mechanism: Allosteric MEK1/2 inhibitor, cutting the RAS-driven growth signal below RAF.
Selumetinib.otherUses: Approved for symptomatic, inoperable plexiform neurofibromas in children with neurofibromatosis type 1.

Alisertib.mechanism: Selective Aurora A kinase inhibitor. Aurora A organises the spindle that separates chromosomes, so blocking it causes catastrophic, lethal mitosis.
Alisertib.otherUses: Investigated in lymphoma and small-cell lung cancer; not approved.

Volasertib.mechanism: Inhibits polo-like kinase 1, a master regulator of mitotic entry and exit, arresting dividing cells and driving them to apoptosis.
Volasertib.otherUses: Investigated in AML, including in older patients with cytarabine; not approved.

Idelalisib.developer: Calistoga Pharmaceuticals, acquired by Gilead Sciences.
Idelalisib.mechanism: Selectively inhibits the delta isoform of PI3K, which is largely restricted to leukocytes — so it targets B-cell survival signalling with less effect on other tissues.
Idelalisib.otherUses: Approved for relapsed chronic lymphocytic leukemia and follicular B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

Rapamycin.developer: Isolated in 1972 by Ayerst Research Laboratories from Streptomyces hygroscopicus found in soil from Rapa Nui (Easter Island), which gave the drug its name.
Rapamycin.mechanism: Binds the protein FKBP12; that pair then clamps mTORC1, shutting down the growth-and-protein-synthesis programme cells run when nutrients are plentiful.
Rapamycin.otherUses: Approved as sirolimus to prevent kidney transplant rejection, and for lymphangioleiomyomatosis; also used on drug-eluting coronary stents.

17-AAG.developer: Developed at the US National Cancer Institute as a less toxic analogue of the natural product geldanamycin.
17-AAG.mechanism: Inhibits HSP90, the chaperone that folds and stabilises many cancer-driving kinases. Without it those client proteins — including mutant FLT3 — are degraded wholesale.
17-AAG.otherUses: Investigated across many cancers; development was limited by liver toxicity and formulation problems. Not approved.

Vorinostat.developer: Merck, from chemistry by Ronald Breslow at Columbia University with Paul Marks at Memorial Sloan Kettering.
Vorinostat.mechanism: Histone deacetylase inhibitor — its hydroxamic acid grabs the zinc ion in the enzyme's active site, leaving chromatin acetylated and gene expression reprogrammed.

Doramapimod.mechanism: A slow, tight-binding allosteric inhibitor of p38 MAP kinase, the stress-and-inflammation signalling node.
Doramapimod.otherUses: Investigated for rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn's disease; not approved.

Ralimetinib.mechanism: Selective p38 MAP kinase inhibitor, blocking a stress-response pathway that supports tumour survival.
Ralimetinib.otherUses: Investigated in ovarian cancer and glioblastoma; not approved.

BEZ235.mechanism: Hits PI3K and mTOR together, closing the feedback loop that lets tumours escape when only one of the two is blocked.
BEZ235.otherUses: Investigated in advanced solid tumours; development discontinued.

GDC-0941.developer: Piramed Pharma with Genentech; also called pictilisib.
GDC-0941.mechanism: Pan-class-I PI3K inhibitor, blocking the pathway that relays growth-factor signals to AKT.
GDC-0941.otherUses: Investigated in breast and lung cancer; not approved.

PI-103.developer: Originated as a chemical probe from Piramed/Genentech PI3K chemistry.
PI-103.mechanism: Dual PI3K and mTOR inhibitor; widely used in the laboratory to test dependence on this pathway.
PI-103.otherUses: A tool compound; poor pharmacological properties kept it out of the clinic.

INK-128.developer: Intellikine, later Takeda; also called sapanisertib or MLN0128.
INK-128.mechanism: Blocks the mTOR kinase itself, so it shuts down both mTORC1 and mTORC2 — unlike rapamycin, which leaves mTORC2 largely untouched.
INK-128.otherUses: Investigated in solid tumours and haematological cancers; not approved.

AT7519.developer: Astex Pharmaceuticals, found by fragment-based screening.
AT7519.mechanism: Multi-CDK inhibitor; its anti-leukemia effect comes largely from CDK9 blockade shutting off transcription of the survival protein MCL-1.
AT7519.otherUses: Investigated in multiple myeloma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia; not approved.

Roscovitine.developer: Developed as seliciclib by Cyclacel Pharmaceuticals.
Roscovitine.mechanism: Purine-based CDK inhibitor competing at the ATP site of CDK2, CDK7 and CDK9.
Roscovitine.otherUses: Investigated in lung cancer, nasopharyngeal carcinoma and cystic fibrosis; not approved.

Staurosporine.developer: Isolated in 1977 from the bacterium Streptomyces staurosporeus by Satoshi Ōmura and colleagues.
Staurosporine.mechanism: Binds the ATP pocket shared by almost every protein kinase, so it inhibits hundreds of them at once. That total lack of selectivity is exactly why it is used: it is the positive control that should kill any sample.
Staurosporine.otherUses: Far too toxic to be a medicine. Its chemistry was the starting point for midostaurin.
Staurosporine.activeIngredient: Staurosporine — a bacterial natural product, not formulated as a medicine

Tofacitinib.mechanism: Inhibits JAK1 and JAK3, damping the cytokine signalling that drives immune activation.
Tofacitinib.otherUses: Approved for rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ulcerative colitis, ankylosing spondylitis and polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

Regorafenib.mechanism: A close chemical relative of sorafenib with one extra fluorine, broadening its reach across VEGFR, TIE2, KIT, RET, RAF and PDGFR.
Regorafenib.otherUses: Approved for metastatic colorectal cancer, gastrointestinal stromal tumour and hepatocellular carcinoma.

Pazopanib.mechanism: Inhibits VEGFR1-3, PDGFR and KIT, working mainly by starving tumours of new blood vessels.
Pazopanib.otherUses: Approved for advanced renal cell carcinoma and advanced soft-tissue sarcoma.

Tivozanib.developer: Kyowa Hakko Kirin, developed by AVEO Oncology.
Tivozanib.mechanism: A very selective VEGFR1-3 inhibitor; the narrow target range is intended to reduce off-target toxicity relative to broader angiogenesis drugs.
Tivozanib.otherUses: Approved for relapsed or refractory advanced renal cell carcinoma.

Linifanib.mechanism: Selective inhibitor of the VEGF and PDGF receptor families, with activity against FLT3.
Linifanib.otherUses: Investigated in hepatocellular and renal cell carcinoma; not approved.

KW-2449.mechanism: Multi-kinase inhibitor of FLT3, ABL and Aurora kinases — combining a growth-signal block with disruption of cell division.
KW-2449.otherUses: Investigated in AML, myelodysplastic syndrome and chronic myeloid leukemia; not approved.

Vargetef.developer: Boehringer Ingelheim. This is nintedanib, sold as Vargatef and Ofev.
Vargetef.mechanism: A triple angiokinase inhibitor blocking VEGFR, FGFR and PDGFR simultaneously, cutting off three separate routes tumours use to recruit blood vessels.
Vargetef.otherUses: Approved for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and other progressive fibrosing interstitial lung diseases, and in the EU with docetaxel for advanced non-small-cell lung adenocarcinoma.

Cytarabine.developer: Synthesised in 1959 at Upjohn, inspired by unusual nucleosides found in the Caribbean sponge Tectitethya crypta.
Cytarabine.mechanism: A cytosine analogue with the wrong sugar. Cells build it into DNA during replication, where it jams DNA polymerase and stalls the replication fork — so it kills whichever cells are dividing fastest.
Cytarabine.otherUses: The backbone of AML induction chemotherapy for fifty years; also used in acute lymphoblastic leukemia, chronic myeloid leukemia in blast crisis, and lymphoma.

Nutlin-3a.developer: Roche, discovered at its Nutley, New Jersey site — which is where the name comes from.
Nutlin-3a.mechanism: Occupies the pocket on MDM2 where p53 normally docks. Freed from MDM2, p53 accumulates and triggers arrest or apoptosis — which only works if the cell still has intact p53.
Nutlin-3a.otherUses: A tool compound that validated MDM2-p53 as a drug target and led to clinical MDM2 inhibitors.
Nutlin-3a.activeIngredient: Nutlin-3a — the active enantiomer of nutlin-3

AGI-5198.mechanism: Inhibits mutant IDH1 specifically. Mutant IDH1 manufactures the metabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate, which blocks the enzymes that let blood cells mature; blocking it lets differentiation resume.
AGI-5198.otherUses: A research probe; the same programme produced the approved IDH1 inhibitor ivosidenib.

AGI-6780.mechanism: Allosteric inhibitor of mutant IDH2, binding at the interface between the two halves of the enzyme and stopping production of 2-hydroxyglutarate.
AGI-6780.otherUses: A research probe; the same programme produced the approved IDH2 inhibitor enasidenib.

BMS-754807.mechanism: Inhibits the insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor and the closely related insulin receptor, cutting a growth and survival signal many tumours co-opt.
BMS-754807.otherUses: Investigated in solid tumours; not approved.

PH-797804.mechanism: Selective inhibitor of the alpha isoform of p38 MAP kinase, the main inflammatory arm of that pathway.
PH-797804.otherUses: Investigated in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and rheumatoid arthritis; not approved.

A-674563.mechanism: Inhibits AKT1 along with PKA and CDK2, blocking the main survival pathway downstream of PI3K.
A-674563.otherUses: A tool compound; not developed clinically.

PP242.developer: Developed as a chemical probe in academic kinase chemistry, later associated with Intellikine.
PP242.mechanism: ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitor blocking both mTORC1 and mTORC2, used to distinguish rapamycin-sensitive from rapamycin-insensitive mTOR functions.
